title: Physiological strategies explain mortality differences among ecologically and culturally significant Australian desert plants following a hotter drought
content:
Abstract
Climate change-induced drought and heatwave events (hotter droughts) are causing mass plant dieback events globally. Recently, Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park (UKTNP) in central Australia experienced a widespread plant dieback (mortality) event. Anangu (Traditional Owners) are concerned about the resulting negative impacts to ecosystems and wish to understand more about the underlying causes of mass plant death. With a focus on ecologically and culturally significant species chosen by Anangu, we measured morphological and physiological traits to characterize differences in physiological strategy underpinning the patterns of dieback observed at UKTNP. Maintenance of leaf relative water content (RWC) was the leaf trait that best predicted dieback severity, with all species that had low levels of dieback exhibiting drought-avoidance strategies where RWC was maintained between spring and summer. Most species with moderate and high levels of dieback exhibited drought-tolerance strategies, evidenced by large declines in seasonal RWC and higher wood densities. However, two small shrub species with high dieback severity may have died due to failure of different physiological mechanisms—one of hydraulic failure via drought tolerance and one of carbon limitation via drought avoidance—highlighting the importance of considering species-specific trait combinations to understand drivers of mortality. Understanding the drivers of dieback will help to support Anangu-led land stewardship and conserve the natural and cultural values of this important landscape.
